blocks.text: It is proved that the word לטאה letaa signifies a lizard, similar to the stellio, extremely venomous and clinging to the ground, which in Arabic is called وحرة [waḥra] vvachara.

Some of the more recent writers try to interpret the Hebrew לטאה letaa from the Greek language, in which λὼτ [lōt] is the mole. Hesychius: Λώτ· ἀσπάλαξ, μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [Lōt· aspalax, mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn]. And λάταξ [latax] is an amphibious animal, akin to the beaver and the otter, of which the Philosopher speaks in History, book 8, chapter 5. Thus in their view לטאה letaa would be either the mole or the latax. Others prefer the shrew-mouse, into which Λητὼ [Lētō], that is, Latona, is fabled to have been changed, on account of the allusion between the words Λητὼ [Lētō] and letaa, which would be the μυγάλη [mygalē]. And it is indeed true that Latona is fabled to have been changed into a shrew-mouse for fear of Typhon. Antoninus Liberalis, Metam. 28: Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις· Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθύς· Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος [Apollōn men egeneto hierax, Hermēs de ibis; Arēs de lepidōtos ichthys; Artemis de ailouros] (not σίλουρος [silouros], as our editions wrongly have it). Τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος· ἔλλῳ δ᾽ Ἡρακλῆς· βοῒ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος· μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ [Tragō de eikazetai Dionysos; ellō d᾽ Hēraklēs; boi d᾽ Hēphaistos; mygalē de Lētō]. But it does not follow from this that the word letaa signifies the shrew-mouse, any more than the mole or the latax because λὼτ [lōt] and λάταξ [latax] sound alike. For the mole has already been dealt with in the preceding verse. And the latax cannot be counted among the reptiles of the earth (any more than the beaver, discussed above) ^{a)}, since it lives rather in the water and has hair partly like that of the seal. It is better, therefore, to follow the ancients, who also number this animal among the species of lizards. Thus for the Greeks it is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] or ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs], and for Jerome the stellio; for Jonathan שממיתא semamitha, which is the [II, 498] very same thing; for the Syrian ܨܪܘܪܝܬܐ tseruritha, that is, the salamander, as they claim; and for the Arabs العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] aladha or العظاية [al-ʿaẓāya] aladhaja, the lizard. So also Solomon [Rashi], Kimchi and the Pomarium. That the Talmudists also took it so is clear from the tractate Oholoth (ch. 1, fol. 45 b), where certain beasts and birds are said to quiver after the head has been cut off, כגון הזנב של הלטאה שהיא מפרכסת, like the tail of the letaa, which (when cut off) still keeps moving. To this the words in the Porta coeli allude: ויש מב״ח אם יכרתו מזנבותיהם יתנועעו זמן רב אחר כן כזנב הלטאה וזנבות השרצים, There are certain animals whose tails, if cut off, move for some time, like the tail of the letaa and of other reptiles. Of the same kind is what Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 23, and Phile, chapter 53, assert: that when a lizard is cut in two by the blow of a rod, each part lives and crawls on two feet, and sometimes they grow together again. I would not, however, lightly believe what is said in the Porta coeli about tails so cut off, כי הן יגדלו אחרי כריתותם, that they grow after being cut off, since it is held as established that once divided they live only a very short time.

So far, then, it is established that the letaa belongs to the lizard kind, since the ancients so determine with great agreement. But to define the species is not for just anyone. The Syrian explains it as the salamander. Of the more recent writers some prefer the stellio, others the lizard. The [col. 1074] former is followed by Pagninus, Arias, Junius, Castalio; the latter by Munster, Schindler, the Genevans, the English, the Italians. I understand a species of lizard which in Arabic is called وحرة [waḥra] wachra or wachara. Concerning it the Arabs note chiefly three things: 1. That it is similar to the stellio. 2. That it clings very closely to the ground. 3. That whatever food it treads on is infected with its venom. These three settle the matter, as we shall show later. But first the Arabs must be heard. Giauhari: الوحرة دويبة حمرا تلتصق بالارض كالعظا [al-waḥra duwaybba ḥamrā taltaṣiqu bi-l-arḍ ka-l-ʿaẓā] Alvvachra, a small red animal, clinging to the ground, like a lizard. Damir: هي دويبة شبيهة بسام ابرص تلتصق بالارض او ضرب من العظا لا تطا طعاما ولا سرابا الا سميته [hiya duwaybba shabīha bi-sām abraṣ taltaṣiqu bi-l-arḍ aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā lā taṭaʾ ṭaʿāman wa-lā sarāban illā sammathu] It is a small animal, similar to the sammabras (or greater stellio), clinging to the ground, or a species of lizard, infecting with its venom whatever food or drink it treads on. In the same place others say: وقيل هي علي شكل سام ابرص [wa-qīla hiya ʿalī shakl sām abraṣ] It is said to be of the form of the sammabras. And Alcamus: الوحرة وزغة كسام ابرص او ضرب من العظا لا تطا شي لا سميته [al-waḥra wazagha ka-sām abraṣ aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā lā taṭaʾ shay lā sammathu] Alvvachara is a guezga, like the sammabras, or a species of lizard, which treads on nothing that it does not infect. Hence وحر [waḥira] vvachara is a verb meaning to infect with venom. Accordingly they say: وحر الصدر عشه ووسواسه [waḥira al-ṣadr ʿishshuhu wa-waswāsuhu] [II, 499] His deceit and his insinuation infected the breast. Likewise: الغل اللازق به كما تلزق الوحرة بالارض [al-ghill al-lāziq bihi kamā talzaqu al-waḥra bi-l-arḍ] Deceit clings to him, as the alvvachara clings to the ground.
